Ultimately, the person who settles for being "well-known" without specific credited results is running a popularity contest with no prize.

point.gentle: **Strategic delegation means keeping the visible step for yourself.** Don't just hand off tasks to save time. Hand off the invisible work and keep the part that everyone sees: the presentation, the announcement, the delivery.
point.direct: **Delegate the groundwork. Own the delivery.** The strategic move isn't offloading tasks randomly. It's offloading the parts nobody sees while keeping the moment when the audience pays attention.
point.competitive: **The visible step is the only step that counts.** Delegate research, prep, and grunt work. Keep the presentation, the announcement, the moment when eyes are on the result. That's where credit is won or lost.

moreDetails.gentle: Not all delegation is equal. Handing off a task to save time is one thing. Handing off the invisible parts while keeping the visible parts is something else entirely. The visible step, whether it is the presentation, the email announcement, or the final delivery to the client, is where the audience forms its impression. That is the moment when credit is assigned. If you delegate that moment, you have given away the single highest-value part of the entire project. The skill is in recognizing which pieces of work are seen by the audience that matters, and making sure those pieces stay in your hands.
moreDetails.direct: Delegation becomes strategic when it is organized around visibility. The tasks no one sees, data gathering, drafting, formatting, logistics, are the ones to hand off. The task everyone sees, the presentation, the delivery, the final sign-off, is the one to keep. This is not about avoiding hard work. It is about understanding that the audience's memory is built from a single moment: the moment the result appears. Whoever is holding the result at that moment gets the credit. Structure your delegation around that fact, and every project you touch reinforces your reputation instead of someone else's.
moreDetails.competitive: There are two kinds of delegation: dumb delegation, where you hand off random tasks to free up time, and strategic delegation, where you hand off everything the audience will never see and keep the one moment they will remember. The difference between these two approaches is the difference between someone who is always busy and someone who is always credited. The visible step is the only step that registers in anyone's memory. In practice, if you are not the person holding the result when the audience is watching, you are subsidizing someone else's career with your labor.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
There's a photograph of Edison's Menlo Park lab that shows rows of workbenches, chemicals, and equipment. What it doesn't show are the dozens of engineers who spent their days at those benches running experiments that would later carry Edison's name. Nikola Tesla was one of them. Tesla redesigned Edison's direct current generators over several grueling months, was promised $50,000, and got told the promise was a joke. The story stings. It's also the clearest illustration of how power really distributes credit.

The psychology behind Law 7 rests on a cognitive bias researchers call the "spotlight effect" mixed with attribution error. People remember the person who was visible at the moment of the outcome. They assume that person caused the outcome. This is why politicians get credit for economic trends they didn't create, why CEOs receive praise for products their teams built, and why Shakespeare is considered a genius storyteller while the writers he borrowed from are barely known. The mechanism isn't fairness. It's perception. And perception follows visibility at the decisive moment.

Here's the honest limitation: this law has a shelf life if you misuse it. People who take credit without ever delivering value eventually get exposed. Edison could sustain the strategy because his lab genuinely produced results, even if the individual credit was misallocated. Shakespeare could borrow plots because he transformed them with language no one else could match. The law works when you add real value at the visible step, not when you add nothing. Pure credit theft without contribution collapses the moment a single insider speaks up. The distinction matters: use others' work, but make the final product genuinely better because you touched it.

Chapter 5 showed that reputation is the cornerstone of power. Chapter 6 argued that attention is how you build that reputation. Law 7 adds the third piece: attention and reputation only compound when they're connected to specific outcomes you can claim. Without credited results, attention fades and reputation stays generic. Edison understood this chain perfectly. He didn't just get attention. He attached his name to products people could buy, hold, and point to. Each credited invention reinforced his reputation, which attracted more attention, which made the next credit capture easier. It's a flywheel.

The deeper read on this law is that it challenges the Western belief in meritocracy as a self-executing system. Merit doesn't announce itself. Someone has to announce it. The person who announces it gets to shape the narrative. If you wait for your work to "speak for itself," you're handing narrative control to whoever steps in front of the microphone first. That's not cynicism. It's the operating system of every organization, team, and creative field you'll encounter. The question isn't whether you'll play this game. One additional wrinkle: the people who are best at this are often the ones who learned it through failure, because the conceptual understanding alone lacks the visceral calibration that comes from having misjudged the situation. It's whether you'll play it deliberately or get played by someone who does.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Tesla spent months fixing Edison's generators. Edison pocketed the improvements and laughed off the bonus he'd promised. Tesla left with nothing but a lesson in how credit actually works. That lesson is Law 7, and it runs deeper than simple delegation. It's a theory of how perception creates power.

The psychological machinery here involves attribution bias. When people see a result, they attribute it to the most visible person associated with it. This isn't laziness. It's how human cognition shortcuts complex chains of causation. Researchers Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson have shown that people routinely overweight the role of visible actors and underweight systemic or background contributors. Edison was the visible actor. Tesla was the background contributor. The public's brain did the rest. Shakespeare operated the same mechanism: he took Plutarch's character studies and Holinshed's chronicles, added dialogue and dramatic structure, and became the visible endpoint. The sources became invisible because they weren't at the point of delivery.

The law's failure mode is worth examining carefully. Credit capture only works when the capturer adds genuine value at the visible stage. Edison didn't just slap his name on things. He directed research, chose which projects to fund, and made commercial decisions that shaped what reached the market. His value was curatorial and strategic, not technical. When credit capture happens without any added value, it creates resentment that eventually leaks. Elizabeth Holmes at Theranos is the modern cautionary tale: she captured credit for technology that didn't exist. The strategy collapsed because there was no real output at the visible step. The law requires substance at the point of claim.

Three chapters form a connected argument here. Chapter 5 established reputation as the base layer of power. Chapter 6 made attention the mechanism for building that reputation. Law 7 converts attention into credited results that reinforce reputation. Without this conversion step, you have visibility without substance: a brand with no product. Edison ran this full cycle: his reputation attracted press, press gave him attention, and he channeled that attention into specific credited inventions. Each cycle made the next one easier. Strip out any one element and the flywheel breaks.

The deepest tension in this law is its conflict with meritocratic ideals. Most people are taught that good work gets recognized automatically. It doesn't. Recognition is a separate activity from production. The people who understand this invest time in both. The people who don't understand it produce excellent work and then feel bitter when someone else gets the recognition. Greene isn't saying fairness doesn't matter. He's saying it doesn't execute itself. If you want your work to be recognized, you need to control the moment of visibility. Merit is the engine. Credit capture is the transmission. Pull back further and you notice that this law interacts with almost every other law in the book, sometimes reinforcing them and sometimes creating genuine dilemmas where two valid principles point in opposite directions. One without the other leaves you stuck.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Tesla outperformed Edison in raw engineering ability. Edison outperformed Tesla in credit capture. Tesla died in a hotel room with pigeons. Edison died as one of the most famous Americans in history. The scoreboard tells you which skill the world rewards.

The psychology is precise. Attribution bias causes people to assign causation to the most visible person at the moment of the outcome. Gilbert and Wilson's research on "correspondence bias" shows that humans systematically overweight individual actors and underweight situational factors. Edison was the individual actor the press could photograph. Tesla was the situational factor. Shakespeare was the playwright whose name appeared on the marquee. Plutarch was the ancient historian whose name appeared in footnotes. The cognitive shortcut is the same in every case: visible person plus visible result equals attributed cause. If you're not visible at the moment of delivery, you don't exist in the story.

This law fails under one specific condition: when the credit capturer adds zero value. Edison directed research priorities, chose commercial applications, and managed the lab's output. His value was strategic, not technical, but it was real. Shakespeare added language, dramatic structure, and emotional depth that his sources lacked. When someone captures credit without adding anything, as Elizabeth Holmes did at Theranos, the scheme collapses because insiders eventually expose the gap. The rule is clear: you can use others' work, but you must transform it. The transformation is both your protection and your legitimate claim.

Chapters 5, 6, and 7 form a power stack. Reputation is the foundation. Attention is the fuel. Credited results are the output that reinforces the foundation. Edison ran all three simultaneously: his reputation attracted journalists, journalists gave him attention, and he converted that attention into named products that strengthened his reputation. Each lap around the cycle widened his lead over people with equal or greater technical skill. This is why Tesla, who arguably contributed more to modern electrical infrastructure, spent decades in Edison's shadow. Tesla had the talent. Edison had the stack.

The hardest truth in this law is that meritocracy is not self-executing. Merit doesn't walk up to a microphone and introduce itself. Someone has to do the introducing. In every organization, the person who controls the introduction controls the narrative. The engineer who ships code doesn't get the feature named after them. The product manager who presents at the all-hands does. The researcher who finds the data doesn't get quoted. The executive who presents the findings at the board meeting does. You can resist this pattern or you can use it. Resistance feels moral but costs you power. The hardest part of mastering this is not the initial insight but the discipline of maintaining it consistently over months and years, when the short-term costs are visible and the long-term payoff is still abstract. The sophisticated version requires holding two contradictory ideas simultaneously: that this principle is generally true and that its exceptions are common enough to require constant recalibration. Using it feels uncomfortable but changes your trajectory.

point.gentle: **Credit capture reshapes relationships over time.** When you consistently take credit, the people whose work you're using will eventually notice the pattern. moreDetails.direct: Meritocracy assumes a functional feedback loop between effort and recognition. No such loop exists automatically. Recognition requires active management: positioning, delivery, framing, and timing. The belief that systems naturally reward the best work is contradicted by every organizational study on promotion patterns, where visibility and self-advocacy consistently predict advancement more strongly than raw performance metrics. Greene's point is not that merit does not matter. It is that merit without active credit management is an unfinished transaction. The work happened. The recognition did not. Closing that gap is a separate, necessary skill.
moreDetails.competitive: Meritocracy is a comforting story that keeps talented people passive while less talented but more strategically aware people collect the rewards. In every organization, the correlation between effort and recognition is weaker than the correlation between visibility and recognition. Promotion studies confirm this repeatedly. The people who rise fastest are not the hardest workers. They are the ones who ensure their work is seen, framed, and credited correctly. Believing the system will recognize you on its own is not nobility. It is a strategic error that your competitors are counting on you to keep making.

activationPrompt.gentle: Before reading, write down the last time you did significant work that someone else got credit for. What specifically did they do to claim the credit? What did you skip?
activationPrompt.direct: Before reading: document one instance where someone captured credit for your work. List the specific action they took at the visibility point that you failed to take.
activationPrompt.competitive: Before reading: write down one situation where someone else got credit for your work. What was their exact move at the moment of delivery? Compare that to what you did at the same moment.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Why does attribution bias make the person at the visible moment of an outcome get credit, even when the real work happened elsewhere?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: What cognitive procedure causes people to assign credit to the visible actor rather than the background contributor?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Why does the human brain systematically over-credit the person at the delivery point and under-credit the people who built the deliverable?

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Name the weakest point in the reasoning using Law 7? When does credit capture backfire, and what specific condition causes the failure?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Under what specific condition does credit capture collapse? What distinguishes Edison's successful version from Holmes's failed version?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: What is the single condition that turns credit capture from a power move into a time bomb? Name the failure case and explain why it failed.

predictionPrompt.direct: Credit is secured. But you're still on offense, still chasing. What strategic problem does the next law solve, and what tool might it use?
predictionPrompt.competitive: You own the credit. But you're still the one making moves, approaching targets, and initiating. What power problem remains, and what does the next law do about it?

retrieve.gentle: Without looking back, explain the difference between Edison's credit capture strategy and Holmes's failed version. What was the key variable that determined success versus collapse?
